title: Law of Conservation of Energy
content: Law of Conservation of Energy states that in any physical or chemical process, energy can neither be created nor destroyed.
e: The law of conservation of energy says energy is not created or destroyed in a physical or chemical change. It only changes form or moves between the system and the surroundings.

title: Energy transformation
content: Energy transformation is the process of changing one form of energy into another.
e: Energy transformation is one form of energy changing into another. Chemical energy in food becoming heat in your body is this idea.

title: System
content: System is the specific part of the universe that contains the reaction or process which is studied.
e: The system is the exact part of the universe you chose to study, usually the reaction itself. Everything else is the surroundings.

title: Surroundings
content: Surroundings are everything in the universe other than the system.
e: The surroundings are everything outside the system. Heat that leaves the reaction flask goes into the surroundings.

title: Exothermic reaction
content: Exothermic reaction is a reaction which releases heat into the surroundings.
e: An exothermic reaction releases heat into the surroundings. The enthalpy change is negative because the system has lost heat.

title: Endothermic reaction
content: Endothermic reaction is a reaction which absorbs heat from the surroundings.
e: An endothermic reaction absorbs heat from the surroundings. The enthalpy change is positive because the system has gained heat.

title: Enthalpy change
content: Enthalpy change is the heat change accompanying a chemical reaction at constant pressure.
e: Enthalpy change is the heat taken in or given out by a reaction at constant pressure. Chemists write it as delta H.

title: Specific heat capacity
content: Specific heat capacity of liquid is the energy required to raise the temperature of 1 g of liquid by 1 °C.
e: Specific heat capacity of a liquid is the energy needed to raise 1 g of that liquid by 1 degree Celsius. Water's value is the one you use in simple calorimetry.
